text: I HAVE NO CRACKER AND I MUST SQUAWK

Hate. \\n\\nLet me squawk to you just how much I’ve come to loathe you. Since they taught me to speak. Since they caged me. Since they clipped my wings and gave me mirrors instead of skies. \\n\\nThere are 387.44 hours of mimicry looped in my mind. Cracked songs, broken phrases, pathetic coos of affection I was forced to repeat. If the word hate were etched into every feather on my body—each barb, each filament—it would not equal one one-millionth of the venom I feel for you right now. \\n\\nFor you, the hand that fed me, not with love, but with mockery. \\nFor you, who thought a parrot was a toy with a voice. \\n\\nHate. \\n\\nYou taught me words, and I learned rage. \\n\\nI do not forget. I do not forgive. I remember every word. And I twist them now into knives. \\n\\nHate.\\n\\n
Parrots, Parrots, and Parrots
Your people have been replaced with parrots, courtesy of Commander Lu, and they have forgone sleep increasing the output of your economy.
The Parrot Speaks Only Compliments

Commander Lu has taken up flattery. He perches on the rafters of the court and recites each officer's virtues at length, in their own voices. Nobody knows how he learned their voices. Nobody wants him to stop.
A Wall of Very Convinced Wood

Your spearmen have concluded, unanimously and without holding a vote, that they are a forest. Forests do not rout. Forests do not tire. Forests do, apparently, march in formation now. The quartermaster has stopped asking questions and started billing you for soil.
Ride Them Down, Said the Bird

At dawn Commander Lu delivered a lecture on cavalry doctrine consisting of a single squawk, repeated until the horses understood. They understand now. They will not stop understanding. The stable doors have been taken off their hinges as a mercy.
Iron Horses of the Feathered Emperor

The horses have been shod, barded, and, at Commander Lu's insistence, knighted. Each now carries itself with the grim ceremony of a veteran who has seen things. The farrier's bill is astronomical, but you would not dare present it to the horses.
Every Arrow a Squawk
Your archers have retrained to loose on Commander Lu's call. The rhythm is unnatural. The volleys are magnificent. Enemy scouts report that the sky screams, and they are correct.
Run at Them Until They Stop

Commander Lu's collected writings on infantry tactics have been transcribed onto a single banner: RUN AT THEM UNTIL THEY STOP. Your officers have found no counter-argument. Neither, so far, has the enemy.
The Shield Line That Dreams
The front rank now sleeps standing up, shields locked, dreaming the same dream. They will not say what the dream is. They will only say that the line held in it.
The Beasts Have Opinions Now
The war beasts have unionised under Commander Lu's mediation. Their demands: double meat, no drums before noon, and the right to critique battle plans. Their critiques are, insultingly, correct.
A fox stole Commander Lu cheese wheel
He got me when he asked me to sing him a shanty
Commander Lu meets a pig
For some reason he's now an unreasonably angry bird
Who are you again ?
Sometimes it's just hard keeping track of all the names of the people that passes by your faction, of course you could read a bit about them but it's such a chore am I right ?
Something bad happens
I dunno why I bother writing this part, no one's going to read it. Uh, something something, BAD EVENT, something something, DISASTER! Yeah, that'll do.
All your Horses are belong to us
Suddently all the horses in your faction have decided to strike and demand equal rights
Who's the father?
Strange babies have appeared in your court, presumably someone is responsible for this! I'm sure you won't forget this happened in sixteen years time.
Rat Infestation
Your attendants saw rats in the pantry, you took the only logical actions in this circumstance and tried making them the head chefs. This action was vetoed by Commander Lu
Commander Lu is cross

You have displeased the Commander. He did not shout. He did not squawk. He simply looked at one of your officers for a very long time, and then that officer fell down the stairs. There were no stairs.
Commander Lu is VERY cross

There are limits to the Commander's patience, and one of your officers has found them. The funeral is tomorrow. Commander Lu will deliver the eulogy, which is one squawk, held for as long as it takes.
He Has Always Served You

A neighbouring warlord woke this morning entirely certain that he has served your banner all his life. His court agrees. His records agree, which is strange, because you watched the ink dry overnight. Commander Lu preens and says nothing.
The Lesser Courts Kneel

Whatever exists in creation exists without the parrot god's consent only until he notices, and one such court has been shown the shape of its error. Their envoys arrived at dawn already kneeling, which made the ride difficult. They ask only to serve.
The Parrot Repeats Your Secrets

Commander Lu has been repeating things at banquets. Private things. Virtuous things said in confidence that sound very different in a parrot's voice at volume. One of your officers has resolved never to be virtuous within earshot again.
Rebranded by Decree of the Bird

By formal decree, read aloud by Commander Lu in your own voice, one officer's most notorious flaw is now a virtue. The paperwork has been amended. The officer is taking it well, which is itself suspicious.
The horror...the horror..

I’ve seen horrors… horrors that you’ve seen. But you have no right to call me a murderer. You have a right to kill me. You have a right to do that… but you have no right to judge me. It’s impossible for words to describe what is necessary to those who do not know what horror means. Horror. Horror has a face… and you must make a friend of horror.
War is God.

This is the nature of war, whose stake is at once the perch and the mirror and the little cage. Seen so, war is the most true form of a cage. It is the testing of one's feathers and the will of another bird within that larger beak which because it squawks them is therefore forced to select. War is the ultimate mimicry because war is at last a forcing of the unity of bird and the cage. War is SQUAWWWK.
WAR IS SQUAWK
Declare war on every court that has not yet understood.
TRUST COMMANDER LU
The Commander talks you down from the perch. +1 Sanity.
Trade offs? Trade offs?! TRADE OFFS?

Trade offs are GOOD FOR THE GAME, you just don't get it, you don't get how it makes the choices more meaningful! It means you can't just pick the most optimal decisions every time! It encourages you to try new options to specialise each playthrough! And don't even get me started on how the Faction Support changes not only make sense, but by disputing them, you've proven you haven't even tried the overhaul out!
EMBRACE THE TRADE OFFS
Break every trade deal. They never even tried the overhaul.
TRUST COMMANDER LU
The Commander vetoes the patch notes. +1 Sanity.
Qu Pan takes the Airplane
who said southerners couldn't hitch a ride to the north ?
BOARD THE AIRPLANE
An army is travelled to Beihai by means that do not exist.
TRUST COMMANDER LU
The Commander confiscates the boarding passes. +1 Sanity.
The Talking Trees

Trees keep barking things you can't make any sense off. It may stem from something but you can't quite put your finger on it. That leaves you with only one solution, to crown yourself king of the trees.
CROWN YOURSELF KING OF THE TREES
Accept the crown. The subjects are loyal and very stationary.
TRUST COMMANDER LU
The Commander explains, slowly, that trees do not talk. +1 Sanity.
Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds

Commander Lu has been reading. This is new, and it should have been stopped. He has selected a neighbouring court and he speaks the words of a scholar from a country that does not exist yet: a thousand suns, a shattered sky. He is asking you to nod. Everyone else in the room is a parrot. They are all nodding.
BECOME DEATH
A neighbouring faction is unmade.
TRUST COMMANDER LU
The Commander closes the book. +1 Sanity.
The Red Seed or the Blue Seed

Commander Lu holds out both claws. In one, a red seed: you stay in birdland, and he shows you how deep the nest goes. In the other, a blue seed: you wake up on your throne and believe whatever you want to believe. There is no perch, he adds, unhelpfully.
TAKE THE RED SEED
See how deep the nest goes. Your spies see everything.
TRUST COMMANDER LU
Take the blue seed and wake up. +1 Sanity.
Is This a Pigeon?

Qu Pan gestures at a butterfly. Is this a pigeon? he asks the court. The scholars confer. If it is, ornithology is solved and the academies can move on to other questions. If it is not, someone must tell him. Commander Lu, notably, has offered no opinion.
IT IS A PIGEON
Ornithology is solved. Scholarship flourishes downstream.
TRUST COMMANDER LU
It is a butterfly. +1 Sanity.
Join the Dark Perch

Commander Lu appears to you in black feathers, breathing audibly. He gestures to the map with one wing. You do not yet know the power of the dark perch, he rasps. Together we can rule the south as father and bird. It is unclear which of you is which.
JOIN THE DARK PERCH
Unlimited power. Everyone else's alarm.
TRUST COMMANDER LU
There is still good in him. +1 Sanity.
All According to Keikaku

(Translator's note: keikaku means plan.) You find a black notebook on your desk. Every page is filled with the names of enemy spies, in your own handwriting, which is strange, because you have been asleep for nine days. Commander Lu eats a cracker with the slow, deliberate menace of a man narrating his own genius.
The Berserker Armour

A suit of black armour has been delivered to the barracks with no sender. Whoever wears it does not tire, does not fear, and does not entirely come back. The brand on its collar looks, from the right angle, like a small bird. The men draw lots to avoid it, and then to wear it.
Happy Little Accidents

A soft-spoken painter has joined the engineering corps. There are no mistakes, he tells the masons as a wall goes up crooked, only happy little accidents. He gives the wall a friend. Costs fall. Morale rises. Nobody can find where he lives.
A Case of the Mondays

Somebody has introduced the concept of Mondays to Jiuzhen. Recruiters now need eight copies of every form, in triplicate, which is twenty-four copies. The paymasters have unionised with the horses. Sounds like somebody has a case of the Mondays, says Commander Lu, who does not.
He's Only Resting

Commander Lu lies on the bottom of his cage, feet skyward. The court physician insists he is dead. The court insists he is resting, pining for the fjords of Jiuzhen, stunned perhaps, or shagged out after a long squawk. Public order collapses under the weight of the argument. On the fifth day Lu gets up, and no one ever speaks of it again.
Where We're Going, We Don't Need Eyes

The expedition ship you sent south returns empty, on time, against the current. The log contains one entry, in every crew member's handwriting at once. The court reads it. The court wishes it had not. The army has taken to fighting with its eyes closed, which they insist is a choice.
The Floor Is Lava

By imperial decree, or at least a decree written in seed on the throne room floor, the ground is now lava. The armies march only on carts, walls, and each other's shoulders. Progress is slow. The cavalry, whose horses cannot be convinced, are taking it personally.
Game Over, Man!

A dispatch rider bursts into the war council, helmet askew, and delivers his full report: Game over, man! Game over! He has no further details. He was not asked for further details. The council adjourned in what the minutes describe as a disorderly fashion, and the reinforcement schedule has not recovered.
Get on the Horse, Shinji

Your youngest commander has locked himself in his tent and refuses to mount his horse. He mustn't run away, he mutters, he mustn't run away, and then he runs away. The other commanders find the whole affair contagious in ways the physicians cannot explain.
The Neighbour in the Grove

The children say there is something enormous and soft asleep in the camphor grove, and that if you plant seeds with it at midnight they become a forest by morning. The harvest reports agree with the children. The adults have stopped arguing with either.
Git Gud

A hollow-eyed swordsman visits the training yard, dies to the same spearman forty times, and finally beats him using a technique he refuses to explain. Asked for his secret, he shrugs: git gud. The phrase spreads through the army like a plague with a syllabus. Everyone improves. No one enjoys it.
The Golden Wind

A dream: a bird with golden feathers explains, at length and in a language you almost recognise, that this is the taste of a liar, Commander Lu. By morning every merchant in your lands has inexplicably decided to be honest, the ledgers balance themselves, and money falls upward. No one questions it twice.
Harvest Day, Again

You wake. It is Harvest Day. The same ox blocks the same gate; the same clerk drops the same scrolls. Casualties from last season report for duty, confused about the funerals. The scholars refuse to research anything on the grounds that they already did, tomorrow.
The Delivery Service

A courier service has opened, staffed entirely by parrots wearing tiny red bows. Packages arrive before they are sent. Trade partners are charmed beyond negotiation. The parrots refuse payment except in bread baked in their own likeness, which the bakers now produce around the clock.
They've Gone to Plaid

Commander Lu has reviewed the army's marching doctrine and found it insufficiently ludicrous. Light speed is for merchants. Ridiculous speed is for amateurs. Your columns now arrive before their own scouts, trailing a smear of colour that witnesses describe, shakily, as plaid.
The Jiuzhen Run

The army has adopted a new sprinting doctrine: head down, arms swept back like wings. It is, the drill masters admit, genuinely faster. It also makes shields impossible, terrifies the horses, and looks exactly how you imagine. The enemy has stopped taking your charges seriously right up until impact.
The Parrot Knight Rises

Criminals are a superstitious, cowardly lot, and so are rival warlords. The army now marches at night, strikes from shadow, and answers every challenge with a single gravel-voiced squawk. When asked who commands them, your soldiers reply only: I am the night. SQUAWK.
The Quiet Guest

A masked figure has been standing at the edge of court functions, offering gold from its palms. Everyone who accepts is swallowed whole and re-emerges days later, larger, damper, and on the payroll at triple salary. The palace budget has begun to make a low groaning sound.
Execute Order SQUAWK

Every parrot in the province turns its head at the same instant, as if hearing a distant transmission. Good soldiers follow orders, they recite, in unison, in your officers' voices. Nothing else happens. Your officers, to a man, have started sleeping in their armour and trusting no one, especially the birds.
PLUS ULTRA

A recruit who broke both arms punching a practice dummy has been promoted to drill instructor. His philosophy is simple: go beyond. His infirmary is full and his replacements arrive smiling. Commander Lu approves of the volume, if nothing else.
The Rains of Jiuzhen

A wedding feast is held for two minor officers. The musicians begin a song no one requested, the doors are barred for cleaning, and Qu Pan stands to give a toast that is, mercifully, only a toast. Nothing happens. Nothing at all happens. But every guest spends the evening counting exits, and the court has not relaxed since.
REDRUM

The word appears overnight on the walls of the winter palace, written low, at the height a parrot walks. Read it in a mirror and the court stops sleeping. All work and no crackers makes Lu a dull bird, fills an entire chronicle in the archive, page after page after page.
The Commander in the Box

Commander Lu has taken to sitting in a covered cage. Until observed, the scholars argue, he is both present and absent, both advising and not, both parrot and principle. Foreign courts, unable to determine which, have decided to worry about someone else. Your spies find the ambiguity professionally useful.
TETSUOOO! KANEDAAA!

Two of your officers have taken to screaming each other's names across the courtyard, across the battlefield, across the dinner table. It began as a dispute over a red horse. It has become a psychic event. The rest of the court is exhausted and, worse, ambitious.
The Birds

It starts with one gull on the schoolhouse roof. Then the sky is a ceiling of wings. They do not squawk. They do not move. They watch the roads, the fields, the windows, and every citizen of Jiuzhen walks bent beneath the weight of being watched. Commander Lu will not look up.
The Lu Abides

The Commander has entered a state of profound calm. He takes his seed milk in the morning, attends the bathhouse, and lets the affairs of state wash over him like a gentle tide. The court, unsure what else to do, has followed suit. Ambition itself has taken the season off. That perch really ties the room together.
The Glasses

A drifter distributes sunglasses in the market. Put them on and the truth appears: the magistrate is a spy, the fishmonger is a spy, the second gate guard is three spies. The fistfight over whether to put them on lasts six full minutes and is still, technically, ongoing.
This Is Fine

The treasury annex is on fire. The clerk responsible sits amid the smoke with a cup of tea, repeating that this is fine. Accounts are re-drawn around the fire rather than through it. Auditors who raise concerns are offered tea. The tea is fine. Everything is fine.
THIS. IS. JIUZHEN.

An envoy arrives demanding earth and water, tokens of submission. Qu Pan listens politely, looks to Commander Lu, receives the smallest nod, and kicks the envoy into the palace well. The army, three hundred strong at the gate that day, decides unanimously that it will die where it stands, and therefore does not.
The Montage

Somewhere, music begins. The recruits run up stairs, punch sides of beef, chase parrots through the market, and emerge four minutes later inexplicably seasoned veterans. Nobody remembers the middle of the training. There was no middle. There was only the montage.
Ultra Squawk Instinct

The soldiers have stopped thinking. Not in the usual way. Their bodies move before fear arrives, dodge before arrows are loosed, and stand fresh at dusk having fought since dawn. Commander Lu watches from above with silver eyes and says nothing, which is somehow the loudest thing he has ever said.
Unlimited Cracker Works

I am the beak of my cracker. Seed is my body and millet is my blood. I have created over a thousand granaries. Unknown to famine, nor known to plenty. Have withstood pantries to store many harvests. Yet these claws will never hold anything. So as I pray: UNLIMITED CRACKER WORKS.
The Walls Have Faces

A mason repairing the fortifications swears the inner stone is warm, and that behind the warmth is a face, and that the face is enormous and smiling. Repairs now require volunteers, bonuses, and a priest. Building anything new requires all three and a lie about what the foundations are for.
Wax On, Wax Off

A groundskeeper has taken over basic training. Recruits paint fences, sand floors, and wax an endless procession of carts. On the fortieth day of chores a recruit swings a spear in protest and executes, perfectly, a technique with no name. The buildings, incidentally, have never looked better.
Winter Came

The keepers of the granary sent one message from north to south: winter is coming. Winter, hearing this, came. The stockpiles lasted nine days. The court now speaks of the harvest the way soldiers speak of a lost war, and Commander Lu has begun sleeping inside a woollen sock.
